skills.title: Identify the variable to change, the variable to measure, and the variables to keep the same
Design a fair test with a control setup for comparison
Explain why repeated trials and averaging make a result more trustworthy

expectations: An investigation starts from a testable question and a prediction with a reason.
In a fair test only one variable is changed on purpose; the effect on another variable is measured; everything else is kept the same.
A control setup is the comparison without the change; it shows what happens anyway, so a difference can be linked to the change.
One trial can be thrown off by chance or a mistake; repeating trials and averaging makes results more reliable, and odd values are checked.
A conclusion says only what the evidence supports, and a test that measures a clue (like light through cloth) is not the same as measuring the real thing (dust).

misconceptions.belief: One experiment, done once, is enough to prove something.
signs: Stops after a single trial and declares the result final
Says 'I did it once, so it is proven'
Ignores a second trial that gives a different value

diagnostic.prompt_en: Kabir shone a torch through a cotton cloth once and saw very little light on the wall. He says, 'Proven: cotton is the best mask cloth.' What is the best response?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kabir ne ek baar torch cotton cloth se chamkaayi aur deewar pe bahut kam roshni dikhi. Woh bolta hai, 'Prove ho gaya: cotton sabse best mask cloth hai.' Sabse sahi jawaab kya hoga?

options.text: He is right; one clear result is proof
He should repeat the test several times and compare other cloths tested the same way before concluding
He should now test each other cloth once and pick the darkest spot

remediation.representation: Results table with Trial 1, 2, 3 and Average columns, where one trial is an odd value
remediation.moveShape: Show a single surprising trial beside three repeats; ask which result they would trust and why

misconceptions.belief: You can change several things at once and still say which one caused the result.
signs: Changes the cloth and the torch distance together
Uses different-sized samples or a different torch
Cannot say which change caused the difference

diagnostic.prompt_en: Cloth A is held 10 cm from the torch and Cloth B 30 cm away. Less light reaches the wall through B. Can we say B blocks light better?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Cloth A torch se 10 cm door hai aur Cloth B 30 cm door. B se deewar pe kam roshni aati hai. Kya hum keh sakte hain ki B behtar roshni rokta hai?

options.text: Yes, less light came through B
No, the distance was also changed, so we cannot tell which change caused it
Yes, because B was tested more carefully from farther away

remediation.representation: Two setup sketches side by side with every difference circled
remediation.moveShape: Spot-the-difference between the two setups; child circles each difference and decides whether the test is fair

misconceptions.belief: A control setup is a waste because nothing is done to it.
signs: Skips the 'no change' setup
Calls the plain setup pointless
Compares the result only with what they expected

diagnostic.prompt_en: Tara wants to test whether dried neem leaves keep insects out of stored flour. She puts neem leaves in one jar of flour. What else does she need?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Tara test karna chahti hai ki kya sookhe neem ke patte rakhe hue aate mein keede aane se rokte hain. Woh ek dabbe mein neem patte daalti hai. Usse aur kya chahiye?

options.text: Nothing; one jar is enough
A second identical jar of the same flour without neem leaves, kept in the same place for the same time
A jar of a different flour with more neem leaves

remediation.representation: Two labelled jars: 'with neem' and 'without neem (control)', same shelf, same date
remediation.moveShape: Ask what she would compare against if insects appeared; let the child invent the control themselves

items.prompt_en: Meera shines the same torch through different cloth samples and looks at the light spot on the wall. What is she changing, what is she observing, and name two things she must keep the same.
items.prompt_hi: Meera ek hi torch alag-alag kapdon se chamkaati hai aur deewar pe roshni ka dhabba dekhti hai. Woh kya badal rahi hai, kya dekh rahi hai, aur do cheezein batao jo use same rakhni chahiye.
items.answer: Changing: the type of cloth. Observing: how bright the light spot is (how much light passes). Keep the same: the torch and its battery, distance from torch to cloth and to wall, number of layers, size of the cloth piece, room lighting.
acceptable: change cloth, observe light, keep torch and distance same
kapda badlo, roshni dekho, torch aur doori same
hints: Ask what is different between one try and the next
Point to what she is watching on the wall
Prompt: she changes the ___, watches the ___, keeps the torch and ___ the same
Assert: change only the cloth; observe the light; keep everything else the same

items.prompt_en: Predict before testing: if you fold the same cotton cloth into two layers instead of one, will more or less torch light pass through? What does that mean for comparing different cloths fairly?
items.prompt_hi: Test se pehle guess karo: agar wahi cotton ka kapda ek ki jagah do tah mein mod do, toh torch ki roshni zyada jaayegi ya kam? Alag kapdon ko fairly compare karne ke liye iska kya matlab hai?
items.answer: Less light passes through two layers. So every cloth must be tested with the same number of layers; otherwise the layers, not the material, could cause the difference.
acceptable: same number of layers for all
hints: Invite them to picture holding up one layer, then two
Point to the gaps in the weave getting covered
Prompt: two layers let ___ light through, so each cloth needs the same ___
Assert: less light; keep layers the same for every cloth

items.prompt_en: Two identical ice cubes sit on two identical steel plates in the same room. You sprinkle salt on one only. Predict which melts first, and say which cube is the control.
items.prompt_hi: Ek jaise do ice cube, ek jaisi do steel plates pe, ek hi kamre mein. Sirf ek pe namak chhidakte ho. Guess karo kaunsa pehle pighlega, aur batao control kaunsa hai.
items.answer: The salted cube melts faster (salt lowers the temperature at which ice can stay frozen). The cube without salt is the control: it shows how fast ice melts anyway.
acceptable: control is the one without salt
hints: Ask why people put salt on icy roads in cold countries
Point to which cube had nothing done to it
Prompt: the salted cube melts ___; the plain cube is the ___
Assert: salted melts faster; the plain cube is the control

items.prompt_en: Predict: if five classmates each time how long an ice cube takes to melt on the same kind of plate, will they all get exactly the same time? Why or why not?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar paanch classmates alag-alag time karein ki ek ice cube ek jaisi plate pe kitni der mein pighalta hai, kya sabka time bilkul same aayega? Kyon ya kyon nahi?
items.answer: No. Small differences in the size of the ice, the spot in the room, and when each person starts and stops the stopwatch give slightly different times. That is why we repeat trials and take an average.
hints: Ask if two ice cubes are ever exactly the same size
Point to human reaction time with a stopwatch
Prompt: times differ a little because ___, so we take the ___
Assert: not exactly the same; repeat and average

items.prompt_en: Three trials of how long an ice cube takes to melt gave 12 minutes, 14 minutes and 13 minutes. What is the average time?
items.prompt_hi: Ice cube pighalne ke teen trials mein 12 minute, 14 minute aur 13 minute aaye. Average time kitna hai?
hints: Ask what 'average' means in their own words
Point to adding all three first
Assert: 39 ÷ 3 = 13 minutes

items.prompt_en: You said Tara needs a second jar of flour without neem leaves. Why is that jar needed?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha Tara ko bina neem patte wala doosra dabba chahiye. Woh dabba kyon zaroori hai?
items.answer: It is the control: it shows what happens to the flour without neem under the same conditions, so any difference can be linked to the neem leaves and not to the weather, the flour or the shelf.
hints: Ask what she would conclude if both jars got insects
Point to the word 'compare'
Prompt: the plain jar shows what happens ___ neem
Assert: it is the control for comparison

items.prompt_en: Two plans to test whether sugar dissolves faster in warm water. Plan A: a glass of warm water and a glass of cold water, same amount of water, same spoon of sugar, both stirred the same way. Plan B: a big glass of warm water that is stirred, and a small glass of cold water that is not stirred. Which plan is fair, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Cheeni garam paani mein jaldi ghulti hai ya nahi, iske do plan. Plan A: ek glass garam paani, ek glass thanda, paani barabar, cheeni ek-ek chammach, dono ek jaise hilaaye. Plan B: bada glass garam paani jo hilaaya gaya, aur chhota glass thanda paani jo hilaaya nahi. Kaunsa plan fair hai, aur kyon?
items.answer: Plan A is fair because only the temperature is different. Plan B also changes the amount of water and the stirring, so we could not tell which change made the sugar dissolve faster.
hints: Ask them to list every difference in Plan B
Point to stirring and glass size
Prompt: in Plan A only the ___ changes
Assert: Plan A, because only one thing changes

items.prompt_en: Your friend wants to test which brand of ball pen writes the longest line before running out. Name the variable to change, the one to measure, and two to keep the same.
items.prompt_hi: Tumhara dost test karna chahta hai ki kaunse brand ka ball pen khatam hone se pehle sabse lambi line likhta hai. Badalne wala variable, naapne wala, aur do same rakhne wale batao.
items.answer: Change: the pen brand. Measure: total length of line written (or pages filled) before it runs out. Keep the same: type of paper, pressure and speed of writing (same person or a guide), new refills of the same size.
acceptable: brand badlo, line ki lambai naapo
hints: Ask what the question is comparing
Point to how they would know which pen 'won'
Prompt: change the ___, measure the ___, keep the ___ the same
Assert: change brand; measure line length; same paper and writing style

items.prompt_en: An advert says: 'Our tonic made a child grow 5 cm taller in one year!' What questions would a scientist ask before believing it?
items.prompt_hi: Ek advertisement kehta hai: 'Hamare tonic se ek bachcha ek saal mein 5 cm lamba ho gaya!' Yakeen karne se pehle ek scientist kya sawaal poochega?
items.answer: Was it only one child (we need many)? Was there a control group not taking the tonic (children grow anyway, often several cm a year)? Were their food, sleep and age similar? Was height measured the same way? Has anyone else repeated it?
hints: Ask how tall a child usually grows in a year
Point to 'a child', just one
Prompt: we need many children and a ___ group without the tonic
Assert: one child and no control proves nothing

items.prompt_en: Turn this into a results table with an average column, then say which cloth blocked the most light. Light-meter app readings (higher means more light): Cloth A gave 7, 6, 7; Cloth B gave 3, 4, 3; Cloth C gave 5, 5, 6.
items.prompt_hi: Ise results table mein badlo, average column ke saath, aur batao kis kapde ne sabse zyada roshni roki. Light-meter app readings (zyada matlab zyada roshni): Cloth A: 7, 6, 7; Cloth B: 3, 4, 3; Cloth C: 5, 5, 6.
items.answer: Columns: Cloth | Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3 | Average. A: 7, 6, 7, average about 6.7. B: 3, 4, 3, average about 3.3. C: 5, 5, 6, average about 5.3. Cloth B blocked the most light (lowest reading).
hints: Ask what the table's first column should list
Point to adding each row and dividing by 3
Prompt: B's average is (3 + 4 + 3) ÷ 3 = ___
Assert: B has the lowest average, so it blocked the most light

items.prompt_en: Golu tested whether music helps plants grow. One pot with music stayed in his sunny room; the other, without music, stayed in a dark storeroom. The music plant grew taller, so he says music helps plants. Spot the flaw.
items.prompt_hi: Golu ne test kiya ki kya music se paudhe badhte hain. Music wala gamla dhoop wale kamre mein raha; bina music wala andhere store room mein. Music wala paudha lamba hua, toh woh kehta hai music se paudhe badhte hain. Galti pakdo.
items.answer: Two things changed: music and sunlight. The difference is most likely due to light, so it is not a fair test. Both pots should get the same light, water and soil, with only music different.
hints: Ask what else was different between the two rooms
Point to what plants need to make food
Prompt: both music and ___ changed
Assert: light changed too, so the test is unfair

items.prompt_en: The torch test shows how much light passes through a cloth. Why might it not tell us everything about how well a mask blocks dust?
items.prompt_hi: Torch test batata hai kapde se kitni roshni jaati hai. Yeh poori tarah kyon nahi bata sakta ki mask dhool kitni rokta hai?
items.answer: Light through the cloth is only a clue about how tightly it is woven. Dust particles behave differently from light, and air (with dust) also leaks around the edges if the mask does not fit. So the torch test is a useful clue, not proof.
hints: Ask what the torch is actually measuring
Point to air sneaking in at the sides of a loose mask
Prompt: the torch test measures ___, not dust itself
Assert: it is a clue about weave, not a direct dust test

items.prompt_en: Teach your younger cousin how to plan a fair test to find which cloth makes the best mask, including why you would test more than once.
items.prompt_hi: Apne chhote cousin ko sikhao ki sabse achha mask cloth dhundhne ke liye fair test kaise plan karte hain, aur ek se zyada baar test kyon karte hain.
items.answer: Key ideas: ask one clear question; change only the cloth; measure the same way each time; keep torch, distance, layers and size the same; keep a comparison; repeat each cloth at least three times and average; check odd results; conclude only what the evidence shows and remember the torch is just a clue.
hints: Invite them to start with the question being tested
Point to what must stay the same
Prompt: change only ___, repeat ___ times, then take the ___
Assert: one change, everything else same, repeat and average

items.prompt_en: From last time: in a fair test, how many variables do you change on purpose?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: fair test mein jaan-boojh kar kitne variable badalte hain?
items.answer: Only one, the one being tested; everything else is kept the same.
hints: Ask what made Golu's music test unfair
Point to 'one change at a time'
Prompt: we change only ___ variable
Assert: just one

workedExample.problem: Does salt make ice melt faster?
steps: Question: does salt make an ice cube melt faster than plain ice?
Predict with a reason: the salted cube will melt first, because salt is used to clear ice from roads
Variables: change salt or no salt; measure the time to melt fully; keep cube size, plate type, place and room the same
Control: an identical cube with no salt, on an identical plate, beside it
Repeat three times, average the times, check any odd value, then say whether the evidence supports the prediction
fadedVersion: Question: does ___ make an ice cube melt faster?
Predict with a reason: the salted cube will melt ___
Variables: change salt or no salt; measure the ___; keep cube size, plate and ___ the same
Control: an identical cube with ___ salt beside it
Repeat ___ times, take the ___, then conclude

skills.title: Organise observations into a table with clear headings and units
Choose and read a bar graph or a line graph
Draw a conclusion the data supports, telling correlation apart from cause

expectations: A results table has column headings with units, and one row for each case or trial.
Bar graphs compare separate categories; line graphs show how something changes over time or as another quantity changes steadily.
A conclusion describes the pattern in the data and says how sure we can be.
Two things happening together (a correlation) does not prove one causes the other; a third factor or chance may explain it.
More data, fair comparison and repeated measurements make a conclusion stronger; odd values are checked, not hidden.

misconceptions.belief: If two things happen together, one must cause the other.
signs: Says 'X went up with Y, so X causes Y'
Never asks what else could explain both
Treats any pattern as proof

diagnostic.prompt_en: In a town, ice-cream sales and the number of sunburn cases both go up in May. What is the best conclusion?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek shehar mein May mein ice-cream ki bikri aur sunburn ke cases dono badhte hain. Sabse sahi conclusion kya hai?

options.text: Eating ice cream causes sunburn
Hot sunny weather increases both; ice cream does not cause sunburn
Sunburn makes people buy ice cream

remediation.representation: Three-box diagram: weather box with arrows to both 'ice cream' and 'sunburn', no arrow between them
remediation.moveShape: Ask 'what could cause both?' and have the child draw the hidden third box

misconceptions.belief: One example is enough to prove or disprove a general pattern.
signs: Uses one relative or friend as proof
Says 'it happened to me, so it's true for everyone'
Ignores larger data

diagnostic.prompt_en: Aman says, 'My uncle never exercises and is fine, so exercise does not matter for health.' What is wrong with this?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Aman kehta hai, 'Mere chacha kabhi exercise nahi karte aur theek hain, toh exercise se health pe koi fark nahi padta.' Isme kya galat hai?

options.text: Nothing; his uncle is real proof
One person cannot show a general pattern; we need data from many people
He should ask one more uncle

remediation.representation: Dot chart with 50 dots showing a trend, and one dot circled as the uncle
remediation.moveShape: Show the one dot inside the big picture; ask what the crowd of dots says

misconceptions.belief: Any kind of graph works for any data, so lines can join separate categories.
signs: Draws a line graph for favourite fruits
Reads between-category values from a line
Chooses graph type by looks

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which data is best shown as a line graph?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsa data line graph se sabse achha dikhega?

options.text: The favourite cricket team of 30 students
The temperature outside recorded every hour from 6 am to 6 pm
The number of students in each section of Class 8

remediation.representation: The same fruit data drawn as bars and as a line, with a question mark between 'mango' and 'banana'
remediation.moveShape: Ask what the line between two fruits would mean; let the child see it means nothing

items.prompt_en: You time how long ice cubes take to melt: three in the sun and three in the shade. What column headings does your table need? Include units.
items.prompt_hi: Tum time karte ho ki ice cube kitni der mein pighalte hain: teen dhoop mein, teen chhaon mein. Table mein kaun se column headings chahiye? Units bhi likho.
items.answer: Place (sun or shade) | Trial 1 time (minutes) | Trial 2 time (minutes) | Trial 3 time (minutes) | Average time (minutes).
acceptable: place, trial 1, trial 2, trial 3, average in minutes
hints: Ask what is being compared
Point to the repeated trials
Prompt: Place | Trial 1 | ___ | ___ | Average, all in ___
Assert: place, three trial times and the average, in minutes

items.prompt_en: A bar graph shows rainfall in a town: June 160 mm, July 290 mm, August 250 mm, September 170 mm. Which month was the wettest, and how much more rain did it get than June?
items.prompt_hi: Ek bar graph mein ek shehar ki baarish: June 160 mm, July 290 mm, August 250 mm, September 170 mm. Sabse zyada baarish kis mahine hui, aur June se kitni zyada?
items.answer: July was the wettest, with 130 mm more than June (290 − 160 = 130).
hints: Ask which bar is tallest
Point to subtracting June from it
Assert: July, 130 mm more

items.prompt_en: Before looking at class data, predict: will students who sleep more always score higher in tests? What else could affect scores?
items.prompt_hi: Class ka data dekhne se pehle guess karo: kya zyada sone wale bachche hamesha test mein zyada score karenge? Score pe aur kya asar daal sakta hai?
items.answer: Not always. Good sleep helps attention and memory, so there may be a general tendency, but scores also depend on study, understanding, health and the test itself, so expect a scattered pattern, not a rule. Even a clear pattern would not by itself prove sleep is the cause.
hints: Ask if anyone they know sleeps a lot but finds tests hard
Point to study time, health and practice
Prompt: scores depend on sleep and also on ___
Assert: maybe a tendency, never 'always'

items.prompt_en: A plant's height is measured once a week: week 1: 2 cm, week 2: 4 cm, week 3: 6 cm, week 4: 8 cm. Predict its height at week 5 if the pattern continues, and say which graph shows this best.
items.prompt_hi: Ek paudhe ki lambai har hafte naapi: hafta 1: 2 cm, hafta 2: 4 cm, hafta 3: 6 cm, hafta 4: 8 cm. Agar pattern chalta rahe toh hafta 5 mein kitni hogi, aur kaunsa graph sabse achha dikhayega?
items.answer: About 10 cm (it grows 2 cm each week). A line graph, because height is changing over time.
hints: Ask how much it grows each week
Point to time on the x-axis
Prompt: 8 cm + ___ = ___; change over time means a ___ graph
Assert: 10 cm; line graph

items.prompt_en: You said ice cream does not cause sunburn. Then why do both go up together in May?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha ice cream se sunburn nahi hota. Toh May mein dono saath-saath kyon badhte hain?
items.answer: A third factor, hot sunny weather, causes both: people buy more ice cream and also spend time in strong sunlight.
hints: Ask what May is like in most of India
Point to something that could push both up
Prompt: both are caused by ___
Assert: hot sunny weather drives both

items.prompt_en: Compare two claims. Riya: 'In our survey of 40 students, those who ate breakfast more often felt less sleepy in first period.' Aman: 'My uncle skips breakfast and is fine, so breakfast does not matter.' Whose evidence is stronger, and what can it still not prove?
items.prompt_hi: Do claims compare karo. Riya: '40 students ke survey mein, jo zyada baar naashta karte the, unhe pehle period mein kam neend aati thi.' Aman: 'Mere chacha naashta nahi karte aur theek hain, toh naashte se fark nahi padta.' Kiska evidence zyada mazboot hai, aur woh kya ab bhi prove nahi kar sakta?
items.answer: Riya's: it uses data from 40 students and shows a pattern; Aman's is one person. But Riya's survey still shows a link, not proof that breakfast is the cause; other habits (like sleep) could differ between the groups.
acceptable: a link, not proof of cause
hints: Ask how many people each claim is based on
Point to the word 'survey'
Prompt: 40 students beats ___ person, but it shows a link, not ___
Assert: Riya's is stronger, yet it shows correlation, not cause

items.prompt_en: Data from one city shows that in weeks when more umbrellas are sold, more people catch colds. Does buying umbrellas cause colds?
items.prompt_hi: Ek shehar ka data dikhata hai ki jin hafton mein zyada chhatriyaan bikti hain, us waqt zyada log sardi-zukaam se beemar hote hain. Kya chhatri khareedne se zukaam hota hai?
items.answer: No. The rainy season is linked to both: rain makes people buy umbrellas, and colds are also common in that season. Correlation is not cause.
hints: Ask when people buy umbrellas
Point to the season
Prompt: both go up in the ___ season
Assert: no; the monsoon is linked to both

items.prompt_en: A cricket coach notices his team has won more matches on days the captain wore a red cap. Should the captain always wear it? How would you check properly?
items.prompt_hi: Ek cricket coach ne dekha ki jis din captain laal topi pehenta hai, team zyada matches jeeti hai. Kya captain ko hamesha woh topi pehenni chahiye? Theek se kaise check karoge?
items.answer: Probably a coincidence: with few matches, chance patterns appear easily, and the cap has no sensible way to cause wins. To check, look at many more matches and at other factors like the opponent, the pitch and home ground.
hints: Ask how many matches the coach looked at
Point to other things that change from match to match
Prompt: a few matches can show a pattern just by ___
Assert: likely chance; check many matches and other factors

items.prompt_en: Turn this sentence into a table and name the graph you would draw: 'At 6 am it was 24 °C, at 9 am 28 °C, at noon 34 °C, at 3 pm 36 °C and at 6 pm 31 °C.' When was it hottest?
items.prompt_hi: Is line ko table mein badlo aur batao kaunsa graph banaoge: 'Subah 6 baje 24 °C, 9 baje 28 °C, dopahar 12 baje 34 °C, 3 baje 36 °C aur shaam 6 baje 31 °C.' Sabse garam kab tha?
items.answer: Table: Time | Temperature (°C) with rows 6 am 24, 9 am 28, 12 noon 34, 3 pm 36, 6 pm 31. A line graph, because temperature changes through the day. Hottest at 3 pm.
hints: Ask what the two columns should be
Point to time moving forward
Prompt: change over time suggests a ___ graph; highest value is at ___
Assert: time and temperature table; line graph; peak at 3 pm

items.prompt_en: Golu made a line graph joining the number of students who like mango, banana, apple and guava. What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Golu ne line graph banaaya jo mango, kela, seb aur amrood pasand karne wale students ki ginti ko jodta hai. Kya galat hai?
items.answer: The fruits are separate categories with no order between them, so a line suggests in-between values or a trend that does not exist. A bar graph should be used.
hints: Ask what a point halfway between mango and banana would mean
Point to the fruits being separate groups
Prompt: separate categories need a ___ graph
Assert: use a bar graph for categories

items.prompt_en: Priya timed a toy car down a ramp: 20 s, 22 s and 58 s. She wrote, 'Average = 33 s, so it takes about half a minute.' What should she have done?
items.prompt_hi: Priya ne ramp se toy car ka time liya: 20 s, 22 s aur 58 s. Usne likha, 'Average = 33 s, toh lagbhag aadha minute lagta hai.' Use kya karna chahiye tha?
items.answer: 58 s is far from the others, so it is probably a mistake (an outlier); she should check what went wrong and repeat that trial. The other two suggest about 21 s, so reporting 33 s is misleading.
hints: Ask which value looks unlike the others
Point to what might have gone wrong in that run
Prompt: the ___ s trial should be checked and ___
Assert: treat 58 s as an outlier and repeat

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend how to go from a messy notebook of measurements to a conclusion they can trust.
items.prompt_hi: Ek dost ko samjhao ki ek bikhri hui notebook ke measurements se aisa conclusion kaise nikaalein jis pe bharosa ho sake.
items.answer: Key ideas: put results in a table with headings and units; repeat trials and average; check odd values; use a bar graph for categories and a line graph for change; describe the pattern; remember correlation is not cause; more data makes it stronger; say how sure you are.
hints: Invite them to start with the table
Point to graphs and odd values
Prompt: a pattern shows a link, but not always a ___
Assert: table, repeat, graph, pattern, careful conclusion

items.prompt_en: From last time: if two things go up together, does that prove one causes the other?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: agar do cheezein saath-saath badhti hain, kya isse prove hota hai ki ek doosre ka kaaran hai?
items.answer: No. It is a correlation; a third factor or chance may explain it.
hints: Ask about ice cream and sunburn
Point to the hidden third factor
Prompt: going together is called ___, not cause
Assert: no, correlation alone is not proof

workedExample.problem: Do students who sleep more score better? Data from 12 classmates.
steps: Collect two values per student: average hours of sleep and their last test score
Make a table: Student | Sleep (hours) | Score (out of 50)
Group students by sleep (less than 7 hours, 7 to 9 hours, more than 9 hours) and find the average score of each group
Draw a bar graph of the average score for each sleep group and describe the pattern
Conclude carefully: a pattern shows a link, but other factors (study, health) could also differ, so it is not proof of cause
fadedVersion: Collect two values per student: hours of ___ and test ___
Make a table: Student | Sleep (___) | Score
Group students by sleep and find the ___ score of each group
Draw a ___ graph of each group's average
Conclude: a pattern shows a ___, not proof of ___

skills.title: Describe the cell as the basic unit of all living things, including plants and microbes
Name the main parts of a cell and how plant cells differ from animal cells
Relate the shape of a cell to the job it does

expectations: All living things are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of life.
Most cells are too small to see without a microscope; some organisms (amoeba, bacteria) are one cell, others have many cells.
Cells usually have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus that controls the cell.
Plant cells also have a cell wall, often chloroplasts and a large vacuole; animal cells have no cell wall.
Cells have shapes suited to their jobs: long branched nerve cells carry messages, long muscle cells contract, disc-shaped red blood cells carry oxygen.
A bigger animal has more cells, not bigger cells.

misconceptions.belief: All cells look the same.
signs: Draws every cell as the same round blob
Is surprised that nerve cells are long
Thinks cell shape does not matter

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement about the cells in your body is correct?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Tumhare shareer ki cells ke baare mein kaunsi baat sahi hai?

options.text: All your cells are round and look the same
Your cells have different shapes, like long nerve cells and disc-shaped red blood cells, suited to their jobs
Only your brain is made of cells

remediation.representation: Gallery card: nerve cell, muscle cell, red blood cell and cheek cell drawn to similar scale with their jobs
remediation.moveShape: Show the gallery; ask the child to guess each cell's job from its shape before revealing

misconceptions.belief: Cells are found only in animals and humans, not in plants or microbes.
signs: Says plants are 'just wood and leaves'
Is surprised by onion peel cells
Does not count bacteria as cells

diagnostic.prompt_en: Under a microscope, a thin onion peel shows many small brick-like boxes. What are they?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Microscope mein pyaaz ki patli jhilli mein bahut saare chhote eent jaise khaane dikhte hain. Yeh kya hain?

options.text: Plant cells, each with a cell wall
Dust grains, because plants do not have cells
Tiny animals living on the onion

remediation.representation: Onion peel micrograph next to a cheek-cell micrograph, both labelled 'cells'
remediation.moveShape: Contrast the two views; ask what both have in common; name Hooke's cork 'cells' as the first plant cells seen

misconceptions.belief: Bigger organisms have bigger cells.
signs: Says an elephant's cells must be huge
Thinks a tree's cells are visible
Links organism size to cell size

diagnostic.prompt_en: An elephant is much bigger than a mouse. Why?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Haathi chuhe se bahut bada hota hai. Kyon?

options.text: Elephant cells are much bigger than mouse cells
An elephant has far more cells; most of its cells are about as small as a mouse's
An elephant has no cells, only organs

remediation.representation: Two walls built from the same-size bricks: a small wall and a huge wall
remediation.moveShape: Ask whether a big building needs bigger bricks or more bricks; map bricks to cells

items.prompt_en: Name two living things made of only one cell and two made of many cells.
items.prompt_hi: Do aise jeev batao jo sirf ek cell ke bane hain, aur do jo bahut saari cells ke bane hain.
items.answer: One cell: amoeba, paramecium, bacteria, yeast. Many cells: humans, a mango tree, a dog, a mushroom.
acceptable: amoeba and bacteria; human and tree
hints: Ask about tiny living things in pond water
Point to their own body as an example
Prompt: amoeba is ___-celled; a mango tree is ___-celled
Assert: amoeba, bacteria are single cells; humans, trees have many

items.prompt_en: Most cells are too small to see with our eyes. What instrument do we use to see them, and who first described 'cells' after looking at thin slices of cork?
items.prompt_hi: Zyaadatar cells aankhon se dikhti nahi. Unhe dekhne ke liye kaunsa instrument use karte hain, aur cork ki patli slice dekh kar 'cells' naam kisne diya?
items.answer: A microscope. Robert Hooke described cells in cork in 1665.
hints: Ask what makes tiny things look bigger
Point to the cork of a bottle
Prompt: a ___ ; the scientist was Robert ___
Assert: microscope; Robert Hooke, 1665

items.prompt_en: Predict before the microscope view: a thin onion peel is placed under a microscope in the school lab. Will we see cells? What shape might they be?
items.prompt_hi: Microscope mein dekhne se pehle guess karo: school lab mein pyaaz ki patli jhilli microscope ke neeche rakhi hai. Kya cells dikhengi? Kis shape ki ho sakti hain?
items.answer: Yes. Many rectangular, brick-like cells packed side by side, each with a clear boundary (the cell wall), and a dark dot (the nucleus) when stained.
hints: Ask whether an onion is a living plant part
Point to bricks in a wall as a picture
Prompt: we will see ___-shaped cells with a thick ___
Assert: yes, brick-like plant cells with cell walls

items.prompt_en: Predict: a nerve cell has to carry messages from your toe all the way to your spinal cord. Would it be round and tiny, or long and thin with branches? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek nerve cell ko tumhare pair ke angoothe se reedh ki haddi (spinal cord) tak sandesh le jaana hai. Woh gol aur chhoti hogi, ya lambi-patli aur shaakhaon wali? Kyon?
items.answer: Long and thin with branches. Its length lets it carry a message over a long distance (some nerve cells are about a metre long), and the branches connect it to many other cells.
hints: Ask what shape a telephone wire has
Point to the distance from toe to back
Prompt: to carry messages far, it must be ___; to connect, it has ___
Assert: long and thin with branches

items.prompt_en: You said onion cells have a cell wall but cheek cells do not. Why do plant cells need a cell wall?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha pyaaz ki cells mein cell wall hoti hai, gaal ki cells mein nahi. Plant cells ko cell wall ki zaroorat kyon hoti hai?
items.answer: The firm cell wall gives the cell shape, support and protection, which helps a plant stand upright without a skeleton.
hints: Ask what holds a tall tree up
Point to plants having no bones
Prompt: the cell wall gives ___ and ___
Assert: support, shape and protection

items.prompt_en: Compare an onion peel cell and a cheek cell. Give two differences and one similarity.
items.prompt_hi: Pyaaz ki jhilli ki cell aur gaal ki cell ko compare karo. Do antar aur ek samaanta batao.
items.answer: Differences: the onion cell has a cell wall and a regular, brick-like shape with a large vacuole; the cheek cell has no cell wall and is flat and irregular. Similarity: both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. (Onion peel has no chloroplasts because it grows underground: not every plant cell is green.)
acceptable: cell wall, shape; both have nucleus
cell wall aur shape; dono mein nucleus
hints: Ask which one belongs to a plant
Point to the outer boundary in each picture
Prompt: only the onion cell has a ___; both have a ___
Assert: cell wall and shape differ; nucleus and membrane are shared

items.prompt_en: Red blood cells are tiny discs with dented middles and, in humans, no nucleus. How does this help them carry oxygen and pass through very narrow blood vessels?
items.prompt_hi: Laal rakt kanika (red blood cells) chhoti disc jaisi hoti hain, beech mein dabi hui, aur insaanon mein inme nucleus nahi hota. Isse oxygen le jaane aur bahut patli naliyon se guzarne mein kaise madad milti hai?
items.answer: The thin disc shape gives a large surface for oxygen to move in and out quickly, and it is flexible enough to squeeze through narrow capillaries. Having no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
hints: Ask why a flat chapati dries faster than a ball of dough
Point to the tight squeeze in tiny vessels
Prompt: the disc gives more ___ and can ___ through narrow tubes
Assert: more surface, flexible, more space for haemoglobin

items.prompt_en: On the underside of a leaf, tiny pores are guarded by pairs of bean-shaped cells. Using 'shape fits job', guess what these guard cells do.
items.prompt_hi: Patte ke neeche ki taraf chhote-chhote chhed hote hain jinke dono taraf sem ke beej jaisi do cells hoti hain. 'Shape kaam ke hisaab se' socho, yeh guard cells kya karti hongi?
items.answer: They open and close the pore (stoma). When they swell with water they curve apart and the pore opens for gases and water vapour to pass; when they lose water the pore closes.
hints: Ask what a pair of doors does
Point to the gap between the two cells
Prompt: when the cells swell, the pore ___
Assert: they open and close the leaf pore

items.prompt_en: Describe the plant-cell diagram you would draw, with five labels. Then say which two labels you would remove for an animal cell.
items.prompt_hi: Plant cell ka jo diagram banaoge uska varnan karo, paanch labels ke saath. Phir batao animal cell ke liye kaunse do labels hata doge.
items.answer: Plant cell labels: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, large vacuole (and chloroplasts). For an animal cell, remove the cell wall and the chloroplasts (and show only small vacuoles or none).
hints: Invite them to start from the outside of the cell
Point to the green parts in a leaf cell
Prompt: animal cells have no ___ and no ___
Assert: remove cell wall and chloroplasts

items.prompt_en: Golu says, 'An elephant's cells must be as big as marbles. That is why it is so huge.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai, 'Haathi ki cells kanche jitni badi hongi. Isiliye woh itna bada hai.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: An elephant is big because it has far more cells, not bigger ones. Most of its cells are microscopic, about as small as a mouse's cells.
hints: Ask whether they have ever seen a single elephant cell with their eyes
Point to bricks in a small wall and a big wall
Prompt: bigger animals have ___ cells, not ___ cells
Assert: more cells, same tiny size

items.prompt_en: Riya says, 'Plants are not made of cells. Cells are only in animals and humans.' Correct her with one piece of evidence.
items.prompt_hi: Riya kehti hai, 'Paudhe cells se nahi bane. Cells sirf jaanwaron aur insaanon mein hoti hain.' Ek saboot de kar use theek karo.
items.answer: Plants are made of cells: an onion peel under a microscope shows plant cells with cell walls, and Robert Hooke first saw cells in cork, which comes from a tree.
hints: Ask what Hooke looked at
Point to the onion peel view
Prompt: onion peel and cork both show ___
Assert: plants are made of cells too

items.prompt_en: Explain to a Class 5 child what a cell is, and why the cells in our body do not all look the same.
items.prompt_hi: Class 5 ke ek bachche ko samjhao ki cell kya hoti hai, aur hamare shareer ki saari cells ek jaisi kyon nahi dikhti.
items.answer: Key ideas: all living things are made of cells, the smallest living unit; most are too small to see without a microscope; cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus; plant cells also have a cell wall; different cells have different shapes for their jobs (long nerve cells carry messages, disc-shaped red blood cells carry oxygen); big animals have more cells, not bigger ones.
hints: Invite them to begin with 'everything alive is made of...'
Point to the nerve cell and red blood cell
Prompt: cells look different because each has a different ___
Assert: cells are the building units; shape fits job

items.prompt_en: From last time: name two parts found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: do aise hisse batao jo plant cells mein hote hain par animal cells mein nahi.
items.answer: The cell wall and chloroplasts (plant cells also usually have one large vacuole).
hints: Ask what gives a plant cell its firm shape
Point to the green parts
Prompt: cell ___ and ___
Assert: cell wall and chloroplasts

workedExample.problem: Why are nerve cells long and branched?
steps: Name the job: carry messages between the brain or spinal cord and far-away body parts, and connect with many other cells
Ask what shape helps travel far: long and thin, like a wire
Ask what shape helps connect to many cells: many branches at the ends
Compare with a red blood cell, whose job (carrying oxygen through narrow vessels) needs a small flexible disc instead
Conclude: a cell's shape fits its job

Shape to travel far: long and ___
Shape to connect many cells: many ___
Compare: a red blood cell is a small flexible ___
Conclude: a cell's shape fits its ___

skills.title: Order the levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
Give examples at each level for humans and for plants
Explain how parts at one level depend on each other and affect the whole

expectations: Similar cells group together to form a tissue that does one kind of job (muscle tissue; xylem in plants).
Different tissues together form an organ with a particular job (heart, stomach, leaf, root).
Organs working together form an organ system (circulatory system: heart, blood vessels and blood).
Organ systems together make up the whole organism.
Each level is built from the level below: organs are made of tissues, not of organisms.
A unicellular organism has no tissues or organs; its single cell does every job.

misconceptions.belief: Organs are made of organisms, or the levels can be in any order.
signs: Puts 'organism' below 'organ'
Skips tissue
Says an organ is made of tiny living things

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is the correct order from smallest to largest?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Chhote se bade ki taraf sahi kram kaunsa hai?

options.text: organism → organ → tissue → cell
cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
cell → organ → tissue → organism

remediation.representation: Zoom ladder: a person, then the digestive system, the stomach, a strip of muscle tissue, a single muscle cell
remediation.moveShape: Zoom in and out step by step; at each step ask 'what is this made of?'

misconceptions.belief: An organ and an organ system are the same thing (the heart is the circulatory system).
signs: Calls the stomach 'the digestive system'
Lists only one organ when asked for a system
Forgets blood and vessels

diagnostic.prompt_en: Is the heart, by itself, the circulatory system?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kya akela dil (heart) hi poora circulatory system hai?

options.text: Yes, the heart is the whole system
No, the heart is one organ; the system also includes blood vessels and blood
No, the heart is only a tissue

remediation.representation: Body outline with the heart highlighted, then the whole network of vessels lit up
remediation.moveShape: Show the heart alone, then the full network; ask what the heart could do without the vessels

misconceptions.belief: Plants do not have tissues, organs or organ systems; only animals do.
signs: Says plants are 'all the same stuff inside'
Does not call a leaf an organ
Thinks systems need a brain

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which of these is a plant organ?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Inme se plant ka organ kaunsa hai?

options.text: A leaf
Nothing; plants do not have organs
A whole mango tree

remediation.representation: Plant body split into root system and shoot system, with leaf, stem, root and flower labelled as organs
remediation.moveShape: Ask what job each plant part does; name each part with a job as an organ

items.prompt_en: Arrange from smallest to biggest: stomach, digestive system, muscle cell, human, muscle tissue.
items.prompt_hi: Chhote se bade ke kram mein lagao: pet (stomach), digestive system, muscle cell, insaan, muscle tissue.
items.answer: Muscle cell → muscle tissue → stomach → digestive system → human.
acceptable: cell, tissue, stomach, digestive system, human
hints: Ask which one is the tiniest
Point to 'tissue' as a group of similar cells
Prompt: cell → ___ → organ → ___ → organism
Assert: muscle cell, muscle tissue, stomach, digestive system, human

items.prompt_en: Classify each as cell, tissue, organ or organ system: leaf, red blood cell, heart, xylem, nervous system.
items.prompt_hi: Har ek ko cell, tissue, organ ya organ system mein baanto: patta, red blood cell, dil, xylem, nervous system.
items.answer: Leaf: organ. Red blood cell: cell. Heart: organ. Xylem: tissue. Nervous system: organ system.
acceptable: leaf organ, rbc cell, heart organ, xylem tissue, nervous system system
hints: Ask which one is a single tiny unit
Point to xylem as the water pipes made of many cells
Prompt: xylem is a ___; a leaf is an ___
Assert: leaf and heart organs; RBC cell; xylem tissue; nervous system a system

items.prompt_en: Predict: if a blood vessel that feeds part of the heart muscle gets blocked, will only that vessel be affected, or the heart and the whole body too? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar dil ki muscle ke ek hisse tak khoon le jaane wali nali band ho jaaye, toh sirf woh nali prabhavit hogi, ya dil aur poora shareer bhi? Kyon?
items.answer: The heart and the whole body. Heart muscle cells there stop getting oxygen and can be damaged (this is a heart attack), so the heart pumps less well and every organ that needs blood can suffer. The levels depend on each other.
hints: Ask what the heart muscle needs to keep beating
Point to the heart supplying every organ
Prompt: damaged cells → weak organ → whole ___ affected
Assert: the whole body can be affected

items.prompt_en: Predict: if a potted plant's roots are badly damaged, will its leaves stay fresh? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar gamle ke paudhe ki jadein bahut kharab ho jaayein, kya uske patte taaze rahenge? Kyon?
items.answer: No, the leaves will wilt and dry. Roots (an organ) take up water, which travels up through xylem tissue to the leaves; the root and shoot systems work together.
hints: Ask where the leaves get water from
Point to the pipes in the stem
Prompt: roots take up ___, which goes up through ___ to the leaves
Assert: leaves wilt; parts of the plant depend on each other

items.prompt_en: You correctly put tissue between cell and organ. Why must tissue come before organ?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne sahi tissue ko cell aur organ ke beech rakha. Organ se pehle tissue kyon aata hai?
items.answer: Because an organ is made of several kinds of tissue working together (the heart has muscle, nerve and other tissues), and each tissue is made of similar cells.
hints: Ask what the heart is made of
Point to muscle tissue and nerve tissue
Prompt: an organ is made of different ___
Assert: organs are built from tissues

items.prompt_en: Compare 'heart' and 'circulatory system'. Which is an organ and which is a system? Name the other parts of the system.
items.prompt_hi: 'Dil' aur 'circulatory system' ko compare karo. Kaunsa organ hai aur kaunsa system? System ke baaki hisse batao.
items.answer: The heart is an organ. The circulatory system is an organ system made of the heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and blood.
acceptable: heart organ; system includes blood vessels and blood
hints: Ask what carries blood away from the heart
Point to the tubes all over the body
Prompt: the system = heart + blood ___ + ___
Assert: heart is one organ; the system adds vessels and blood

items.prompt_en: An amoeba is one cell; a human has trillions. Does an amoeba have tissues or organs? How does it eat and move, then?
items.prompt_hi: Amoeba ek cell hai; insaan mein khurbon cells hain. Kya amoeba mein tissues ya organs hote hain? Toh woh khaata aur chalta kaise hai?
items.answer: No tissues or organs. Its single cell does every job: it moves by pushing out finger-like extensions (false feet) and eats by surrounding food with them.
acceptable: no, the one cell does everything
nahi, ek cell sab karti hai
hints: Ask how many cells an amoeba has
Point to its finger-like false feet
Prompt: in a one-celled organism, the ___ does all jobs
Assert: no tissues or organs; one cell does it all

items.prompt_en: Use the levels to describe your eye: name a tissue it contains, say what level the eye is, and which system it belongs to.
items.prompt_hi: Levels ka use karke apni aankh ke baare mein batao: usme ek tissue ka naam, aankh kis level pe hai, aur kis system ka hissa hai.
items.answer: The eye is an organ (a sense organ). It contains tissues such as muscle tissue (to move the eye and adjust the lens) and nerve tissue (in the retina). It belongs to the nervous system.
hints: Ask what job the eye does
Point to muscles moving the eyeball
Prompt: the eye is an ___, part of the ___ system
Assert: organ; nervous system; has muscle and nerve tissue

items.prompt_en: Compare the levels of organisation to a house: bricks, walls, rooms, a set of rooms working together (like kitchen, store and dining), the whole house. Match each to a level, and say one way the comparison breaks down.
items.prompt_hi: Levels ko ek ghar se compare karo: eentein, deewarein, kamre, kuch kamre jo milkar kaam karte hain (jaise kitchen, store aur dining), aur poora ghar. Har ek ko level se milao, aur ek jagah batao jahan yeh tulna kaam nahi karti.
items.answer: Brick = cell; wall = tissue; room = organ; kitchen-store-dining set = organ system; house = organism. It breaks down because bricks are not alive: real cells grow, use food, divide and do work.
acceptable: brick cell, wall tissue, room organ, set system, house organism
hints: Ask what a wall is made of
Point to rooms that work together for cooking and eating
Prompt: brick = ___, wall = ___, room = ___
Assert: bricks to house matches cell to organism, but bricks are not alive

items.prompt_en: Describe a five-step ladder diagram for a plant, from one cell in the leaf to the whole plant, naming each step.
items.prompt_hi: Ek paudhe ke liye paanch seedhi wala diagram batao, patte ki ek cell se poore paudhe tak, har seedhi ka naam ke saath.
items.answer: Leaf cell (with chloroplasts) → leaf tissue that makes food → leaf (organ) → shoot system (organ system) → the whole plant (organism).
acceptable: cell, tissue, leaf, shoot system, plant
hints: Ask where food is made in a plant
Point to the shoot system above the ground
Prompt: cell → tissue → ___ → ___ system → plant
Assert: cell, tissue, leaf, shoot system, plant

items.prompt_en: Golu's notes say: 'Organs are made of many tiny organisms joined together.' Fix it.
items.prompt_hi: Golu ke notes mein likha hai: 'Organs bahut saare chhote-chhote organisms ke jud jaane se bante hain.' Ise theek karo.
items.answer: Organs are made of tissues, and tissues are made of similar cells. The organism is the whole living thing at the top of the ladder.
hints: Ask what 'organism' means
Point to the ladder order
Prompt: organs are made of ___, which are made of ___
Assert: tissues and cells, not organisms

items.prompt_en: Explain to your younger sister how one cell in your stomach is connected to you as a whole person.
items.prompt_hi: Apni chhoti behen ko samjhao ki tumhare pet ki ek cell poore tum se kaise judi hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: a stomach cell is one of many similar cells forming stomach tissue; tissues together make the stomach (an organ); the stomach works with other organs in the digestive system; all systems together make the whole person; if cells are damaged, the organ, system and person can be affected.
hints: Invite them to start with the single cell
Point to each step up the ladder
Prompt: cell → tissue → ___ → digestive system → ___
Assert: each level is built from the one below

items.prompt_en: From last time: what comes right after 'organ' in the levels of organisation?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: levels of organisation mein 'organ' ke theek baad kya aata hai?
items.answer: Organ system.
hints: Ask what the heart is part of
Point to organs working together
Prompt: organ → organ ___
Assert: organ system

workedExample.problem: Place the heart on the ladder of levels.
steps: Cell: a heart muscle cell, which can contract
Tissue: many heart muscle cells together form cardiac muscle tissue (with nerve and other tissues alongside)
Organ: these tissues together make the heart, whose job is to pump blood
Organ system: the heart with blood vessels and blood forms the circulatory system
Organism: the circulatory system works with all other systems to make the whole human

Tissue: many such cells form cardiac ___ tissue
Organ: tissues together make the ___
Organ system: heart + blood ___ + blood = circulatory system
Organism: all systems together make the whole ___

skills.title: Name the main groups of microorganisms with examples
Explain useful roles of microbes: fermentation, decomposition, nitrogen fixation, medicines
Explain harmful roles of microbes and simple ways to prevent harm

expectations: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope; they live almost everywhere, including inside us.
Main groups are bacteria, fungi (yeast, moulds), protozoa and algae; viruses are even smaller and multiply only inside living cells.

Useful microbes: bacteria turn milk into curd; yeast and bacteria ferment idli batter and dough, making gas bubbles; decomposers turn waste into compost; Rhizobium in pulse roots adds nitrogen to soil; some moulds give antibiotics such as penicillin.
Harmful microbes cause diseases (malaria by a protozoan, TB and cholera by bacteria, common cold and dengue by viruses) and spoil food.
Most microbes are harmless or helpful; harm is reduced by hygiene, cooking, cooling food and keeping it covered.

misconceptions.belief: All microorganisms are germs that cause disease.
signs: Uses 'microbe' and 'germ' as the same word
Wants to kill every microbe
Is surprised that curd is full of bacteria

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement is true?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsi baat sahi hai?

options.text: All microbes are harmful and should be destroyed
Most microbes are harmless or useful, like curd bacteria; only some cause disease
Microbes are found only in dirty places

remediation.representation: Two-column board: 'helpers' (curd, idli, compost, root nodules) vs 'troublemakers' (malaria, cholera, mould on bread)
remediation.moveShape: Let the child sort cards; then ask which column has more examples from their own kitchen

misconceptions.belief: Microbes live only in dirty places; clean things have none.
signs: Says a clean bowl of curd has no microbes
Thinks washing removes all microbes
Is surprised microbes live inside the body

diagnostic.prompt_en: Is there any microbe in a clean bowl of fresh curd?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kya saaf katori mein rakhe taaze dahi mein koi microbe hota hai?

options.text: No, it is clean, so there are no microbes
Yes, curd is full of helpful bacteria that made it
Only if a fly sat on it

remediation.representation: Zoomed-in curd picture showing rod-shaped bacteria among milk protein
remediation.moveShape: Ask how one spoon of old curd turns a whole bowl of milk into curd; let them reason that something living multiplied

misconceptions.belief: Fermentation means the food has gone bad.
signs: Calls sour idli batter 'spoilt'
Thinks bubbles in batter mean danger
Lumps curd with rotten food

diagnostic.prompt_en: Idli batter left overnight becomes bubbly, puffy and a little sour. What happened?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Raat bhar rakha idli ka ghol phool kar bubbly aur thoda khatta ho jaata hai. Kya hua?

options.text: It got spoilt and must be thrown away
Yeast and bacteria fermented it, making gas that puffs it up; this is wanted
Room air got trapped in it by itself

remediation.representation: Side-by-side: fermented batter (planned, wanted) and mouldy rice (unwanted, unsafe)
remediation.moveShape: Contrast the two; ask who 'invited' the microbes in each case and whether the result is wanted

items.prompt_en: Match each microbe to its group (bacteria, fungus, protozoan, alga, virus): yeast; Plasmodium, which causes malaria; Lactobacillus in curd; the green slimy layer in a pond; the microbe that causes the common cold.
items.prompt_hi: Har microbe ko uske group se milao (bacteria, fungus, protozoa, algae, virus): yeast; Plasmodium jo malaria karta hai; dahi ka Lactobacillus; taalaab ki hari chipchipi parat; zukaam karne wala microbe.
items.answer: Yeast: fungus. Plasmodium: protozoan. Lactobacillus: bacterium. Green pond layer: algae. Common cold: virus.
acceptable: yeast fungus, plasmodium protozoa, lactobacillus bacteria, pond algae, cold virus
hints: Ask which one is used to make bread rise
Point to malaria being spread by mosquitoes but caused by a protozoan
Prompt: yeast is a ___; the cold is caused by a ___
Assert: fungus, protozoan, bacterium, alga, virus

items.prompt_en: Predict: a spoon of curd is stirred into lukewarm milk and left overnight. What will you find in the morning, and what does that tell you about microbes?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: gungune doodh mein ek chammach dahi mila kar raat bhar rakha. Subah kya milega, aur isse microbes ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
items.answer: The milk sets into curd. Lactobacillus bacteria from the starter multiply and turn milk sugar into acid, thickening the milk: these microbes are helpful.
hints: Ask what happens at home when curd is set
Point to the tiny spoon of starter
Prompt: bacteria in the starter ___ and turn milk into ___
Assert: it sets into curd; the bacteria are helpers

items.prompt_en: Predict: two bowls of the same dough with a pinch of yeast; one kept in a warm spot, one in the fridge. Which rises more in two hours, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek jaisa aata do katoriyon mein, dono mein chutki bhar yeast; ek garam jagah, ek fridge mein. Do ghante mein kaunsa zyada phoolega, aur kyon?
items.answer: The warm bowl rises more. Yeast is a living fungus that is more active in warmth, producing more carbon dioxide gas; the cold slows it down.
acceptable: yeast is more active in warmth
hints: Ask if yeast is alive
Point to winter when batter takes longer
Prompt: yeast works ___ in warmth and makes ___ gas

expectations: Health means physical, mental and social well-being, not only 'not being sick'.
Physical health is supported by a balanced diet, clean water, at least an hour of physical activity a day, enough sleep (about 8 to 10 hours for teenagers) and hygiene.
Mental health includes handling stress, feeling okay about yourself and asking for help; talking to a trusted adult is a health habit.
Social health means supportive relationships with family, friends and community.
Habits add up over time: late nights, too much screen time and skipped meals can harm health even when you feel fine today.
You cannot judge someone's health just by their body size or looks.

skills.title: Tell communicable diseases from non-communicable ones, with examples
Explain how communicable diseases spread: air, water and food, contact, and carriers like mosquitoes
Explain risk factors for non-communicable diseases and why antibiotics do not cure viral illness

expectations: Communicable diseases are caused by microbes (pathogens) and can pass from one person to another: cold, flu, TB, cholera, typhoid, malaria, dengue.
They spread through the air (coughs and sneezes), contaminated water or food, contact, and carriers (vectors) such as mosquitoes.
Dengue spreads through Aedes mosquitoes that breed in clean stagnant water (coolers, pots, tyres); malaria through Anopheles mosquitoes.
Non-communicable diseases (diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, most cancers) are not caught from others; they develop due to genes, diet, inactivity, smoking, pollution and age.
Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses; the common cold and dengue are viral, so antibiotics do not cure them; medicines are taken only as a doctor advises.

misconceptions.belief: Antibiotics cure viral fevers like the common cold.
signs: Asks for an antibiotic for every fever
Says antibiotics 'kill all germs'
Uses leftover tablets for a cold

diagnostic.prompt_en: Riya has a common cold. A friend says, 'Take an antibiotic, it will cure it fast.' What is correct?

options.text: Yes, antibiotics kill every kind of germ
No; a cold is caused by a virus and antibiotics act on bacteria; rest, fluids, and see a doctor if it gets worse
Yes, but take only half the strip

remediation.representation: Two locks and one key: the antibiotic key fits the 'bacteria' lock but not the 'virus' lock
remediation.moveShape: Sort illnesses into bacterial and viral first; then ask which group the key works on

No; diabetes is non-communicable and is not caused by a microbe
Only if you also eat sweets with them

items.prompt_en: You said the mild fever after a vaccine is not the disease. Why does it happen, then?

expectations: An electric current in a wire produces a magnetic effect around it, which can turn a compass needle.
A coil of insulated wire wound around an iron core and connected to a cell becomes an electromagnet.
An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows; when the current is switched off it loses most of its magnetism.
It becomes stronger with more turns of wire, more current (for example, more cells) and an iron core; aluminium, copper or wood cores do not help in the same way.
Electromagnets are used in electric bells, scrapyard cranes, loudspeakers, motors, MRI machines and electric locks.
Experiments use only low-voltage cells, connected for a few seconds at a time because the wire warms; never mains electricity.

items.prompt_en: In an electric bell, an electromagnet pulls an iron strip carrying a small hammer, which hits the gong. As the strip moves, it breaks the circuit. Explain why the hammer keeps striking again and again while the button is pressed.

items.answer: Key ideas: wind insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a cell through a switch; current produces magnetism, which stops when the current stops; more turns, more current and an iron core make it stronger; it only attracts magnetic materials like iron; a crane can switch it off to drop the load.

skills.title: Recognise that a current in a wire produces heat, and name appliances that use this
Explain what affects how hot a wire gets: material, thickness, length and the current
Explain how fuses and MCBs protect circuits, and the dangers of overloading

expectations: When electric current flows through a wire, the wire gets heated: this is the heating effect of current.
Heaters, irons, geysers, kettles and toasters use elements of materials like nichrome, which oppose current strongly and do not melt easily.
For the same current, a thinner or longer wire, or one of a material that opposes current more, heats up more; a larger current heats any wire more.
A fuse is a thin wire with a low melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large; an MCB switches off automatically and can be reset.
Overloading (too many appliances on one socket) or a short circuit makes a very large current flow, which can overheat wires and start a fire.
Never touch switches with wet hands, never replace a fuse with a thick copper wire, and leave mains wiring to an electrician.

skills.title: Make a simple cell from two different metals and an electrolyte, and say what each part does
Explain that a cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy, and that current flows only in a closed loop without being used up

expectations: A simple cell needs two different metals (electrodes) in an electrolyte such as lemon juice, for example a copper coin and a zinc-coated (galvanised) nail in a lemon.
Chemical reactions at the metals push charges around a closed circuit: chemical energy changes into electrical energy.
One lemon cell gives a little under 1 volt; several joined in series can light an LED.
A battery does not store current like water in a tank; it stores chemicals, and when they are used up it is 'dead'. Current is not used up: the same current flows through every part of a single loop.
A dry cell is used once; rechargeable batteries (lithium-ion in phones, lead-acid in inverters and cars) have their reactions reversed by charging.
Batteries must not be burnt, opened or thrown in household waste; they go to e-waste collection.

Thinks charging pours current in
Cannot say what is inside a cell

skills.title: Describe a force as a push or pull and list its effects on motion and shape
Explain that a moving object keeps moving unless a force such as friction acts on it
Identify balanced forces on still objects and unbalanced forces that change motion

expectations: A force is a push or a pull that comes from an interaction between two objects.
A force can make a still object move, stop a moving one, change its speed or direction, or change its shape.
A moving object does not need a force to keep moving; it slows down because forces like friction and air resistance act against it. With no such forces it would keep moving.
A still object can have forces on it that are balanced: a book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table.
Unbalanced forces change motion; forces in the same direction add up and opposite forces subtract (tug of war).
Force is measured in newtons (N), and non-living things (the Earth, a magnet, a table) can exert forces too.
