items.prompt_en: Predict: you press a rubber ball and a ball of atta dough the same way between your palms, then let go. What happens to each?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: rubber ki gend aur aate ki loi ko hatheliyon ke beech ek jaisa dabaate ho, phir chhod dete ho. Dono ka kya hoga?
items.answer: Both change shape while pressed. The rubber ball springs back to its shape; the dough stays flattened. A force can change shape for a while or for good.
acceptable: rubber springs back, dough stays flat
hints: Ask what happens to a cricket ball when it is squeezed
Point to the dough after letting go
Prompt: rubber ___ back; dough stays ___
Assert: force changes shape, sometimes permanently

items.prompt_en: Predict: you give the same push to a marble on a smooth marble floor and on a carpet. Where does it roll farther? What would happen if there were no friction at all?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek kanche ko chikne marble ke farsh pe aur carpet pe ek jaisa dhakka do. Kahan zyada door jaayega? Agar friction bilkul na ho toh kya hoga?
items.answer: Farther on the smooth floor, because there is less friction. With no friction or air resistance at all, it would keep rolling at the same speed in a straight line.
acceptable: smooth floor; it would keep going
hints: Ask which surface 'grabs' the marble more
Point to the pattern as friction gets smaller
Prompt: less friction, ___ distance; zero friction, it ___
Assert: farther on smooth; without friction it never stops

items.prompt_en: Predict: in a tug of war, Team A pulls left with 500 N and Team B pulls right with 500 N. Which way does the rope move? What if Team A pulls with 600 N?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: rassa-kashi mein Team A 500 N baayein aur Team B 500 N daayein kheenchti hai. Rassi kis taraf jaayegi? Agar Team A 600 N lagaaye toh?
items.answer: At 500 N each, the forces are balanced, so the rope does not move. At 600 N, the net force is 100 N to the left, so the rope moves towards Team A.
acceptable: nahi hilegi; phir A ki taraf
hints: Ask what happens when both sides pull equally
Point to subtracting opposite forces
Prompt: 600 − 500 = ___ N towards ___
Assert: balanced, then 100 N towards Team A

items.prompt_en: You said the marble would keep rolling for ever without friction. Then why do we have to keep pedalling a cycle on a flat road?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha friction na ho toh kancha hamesha ludhakta rahega. Toh phir seedhi sadak pe cycle chalaate rehne ke liye pedal kyon maarte rehna padta hai?
items.answer: Because friction and air resistance keep pushing back on the cycle. Pedalling balances these backward forces; it is not that motion itself needs a force.
acceptable: to balance friction and air resistance
friction ko balance karne ke liye
hints: Ask what happens if you stop pedalling
Point to the wind on your face and the road
Prompt: pedalling balances ___ and ___
Assert: we pedal only to cancel the forces slowing us

items.prompt_en: Compare a book resting on a table with the same book being pushed across the table at a steady speed. What forces act in each case, and are they balanced?
items.prompt_hi: Mez pe rakhi kitaab aur usi kitaab ko mez pe ek jaisi raftaar se dhakelna, dono ki tulna karo. Har case mein kaunse force hain, aur kya woh balanced hain?
items.answer: Resting: gravity pulls down and the table pushes up; balanced. Pushed at steady speed: gravity and the table's push still balance, and your forward push balances friction backward; the forces are still balanced, so the speed does not change.
hints: Ask what the table does in both cases
Point to the steady speed meaning no change in motion
Prompt: steady speed means the forces are ___
Assert: balanced in both; steady motion needs no net force

items.prompt_en: A goalkeeper dives and stops a penalty kick. A striker heads a cross into the goal. Name the effect of force in each case.
items.prompt_hi: Goalkeeper kood kar penalty rok leta hai. Striker cross ko sir se goal mein maarta hai. Har case mein force ka kya asar hai?
items.answer: The goalkeeper's force stops the moving ball. The striker's header changes the ball's direction (and speed).
hints: Ask what happened to the ball's motion each time
Point to the ball's new path after the header
Prompt: keeper ___ the ball; header changes its ___
Assert: stopping and changing direction

items.prompt_en: An astronaut on the space station gives a floating spanner a gentle push. With almost nothing to slow it, what will it do? Why is this different from Earth?
items.prompt_hi: Space station mein ek astronaut tairte hue spanner ko halka sa dhakka deta hai. Use rokne wala lagbhag kuch nahi hai, toh woh kya karega? Yeh Dharti se alag kyon hai?
items.answer: It keeps drifting at the same speed in a straight line until something (a wall or a hand) acts on it. On Earth, friction and air resistance quickly slow moving things down.
hints: Ask what slows things down on Earth
Point to the missing friction
Prompt: with no force against it, it keeps moving at the ___ speed
Assert: it drifts on until something stops it

items.prompt_en: Describe a force-arrow diagram for a box pushed with 30 N to the right while friction acts with 10 N to the left. What is the net force, and what happens to the box?
items.prompt_hi: Ek dabba 30 N se daayein dhakela ja raha hai aur friction 10 N baayein lag raha hai. Iska force-arrow diagram batao. Net force kitna hai, aur dabbe ka kya hoga?
items.answer: A long arrow of 30 N pointing right and a shorter arrow of 10 N pointing left. Net force = 20 N to the right, so the box speeds up to the right.
hints: Ask which arrow should be longer
Point to subtracting opposite forces
Prompt: 30 − 10 = ___ N to the ___
Assert: 20 N right; the box speeds up

items.prompt_en: Golu says, 'A glass of water on the table has no force on it, because it is not moving.' Fix his idea.
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai, 'Mez pe rakhe paani ke glass pe koi force nahi hai, kyunki woh hil nahi raha.' Uski soch theek karo.
items.answer: Gravity pulls the glass down and the table pushes it up with an equal force. The forces are balanced, so its motion does not change, but forces are acting.
hints: Ask what would happen if the table vanished
Point to the sponge squashing under a book
Prompt: gravity pulls ___; the table pushes ___
Assert: two balanced forces act on it

items.prompt_en: Riya says, 'A table cannot push anything; only people and animals can push.' What would you tell her?
items.prompt_hi: Riya kehti hai, 'Mez kisi cheez ko dhakel nahi sakti; sirf insaan aur jaanwar dhakel sakte hain.' Tum use kya bataoge?
items.answer: Non-living things exert forces too: the table pushes up on a book, a magnet pulls a pin, the Earth pulls everything, and a stretched rubber band pushes a paper ball.
acceptable: nirjeev cheezein bhi force lagaati hain
hints: Ask what holds the book up
Point to a magnet pulling a pin
Prompt: the table, a magnet and the ___ all exert forces
Assert: forces come from interactions, not only living things

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger cousin why a football stops rolling, and why it is wrong to say 'the force of the kick ran out'.
items.prompt_hi: Apne chhote cousin ko samjhao ki football ludhakna kyon band karti hai, aur 'kick ka force khatam ho gaya' kehna galat kyon hai.
items.answer: Key ideas: a force is a push or pull; the kick acts only while the foot touches the ball; after that the ball keeps moving on its own; friction and air resistance act against it and slow it down; on a smoother surface it goes farther; with no friction it would keep going; still objects can have balanced forces.
hints: Invite them to start from the moment the foot leaves the ball
Point to the grass and the air
Prompt: the ball stops because ___ acts against it
Assert: friction stops it; motion needs no force to continue

items.prompt_en: From last time: what is the unit of force, and name two effects a force can have.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: force ki unit kya hai, aur force ke do asar batao.
items.answer: The newton (N). Effects: start or stop motion, change speed, change direction, change shape.
hints: Ask about the scientist the unit is named after
Point to the dough and the caught ball
Prompt: the unit is the ___
Assert: newton; start, stop, speed, direction, shape

workedExample.problem: A trolley is pushed with 50 N while friction acts with 20 N. What happens, and what happens when the push stops?
steps: Draw the forces: 50 N forward (push) and 20 N backward (friction)
They act in opposite directions, so subtract: net force = 50 − 20 = 30 N forward
An unbalanced force changes motion, so the trolley speeds up in the forward direction
When the push stops, only friction (20 N backward) acts
So the trolley slows down and stops; it was friction, not a 'used-up push', that stopped it
fadedVersion: Draw the forces: ___ N forward and ___ N backward
Net force = 50 − 20 = ___ N forward
Unbalanced force, so the trolley ___
When the push stops, only ___ acts
So the trolley ___ and stops

skills.title: Classify forces as contact (muscular, friction, normal) or non-contact (magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational)
Explain what friction depends on, when it helps or harms, and how to change it
Explain that gravity acts on all objects all the time and that non-contact forces act across a gap

expectations: Contact forces act only when objects touch: muscular force, friction, the push of a surface, tension in a rope.
Non-contact forces act from a distance: magnetic force, electrostatic force (a rubbed comb attracting paper bits) and gravitational force.
Friction opposes the sliding or rolling of one surface over another; rougher surfaces give more friction.
Friction is useful (walking, writing, gripping, brakes) and also wasteful (wear and tear, heating in machines); it is reduced by oil, wheels and ball bearings and increased by treads and grip.

Gravity is an attraction between all objects with mass; the Earth pulls on everything near it all the time, whether it is falling, resting or moving up, and gravity also acts across empty space (it holds the Moon in orbit).

misconceptions.belief: Friction is always harmful and should be removed everywhere.
signs: Lists only bad effects of friction
Wants frictionless shoes
Forgets that brakes and walking need friction

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which statement about friction is correct?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Friction ke baare mein kaunsi baat sahi hai?

options.text: Friction is always bad; we should get rid of it
Friction is useful for walking, writing and braking, but it also causes wear and heat
Friction only happens on rough roads

remediation.representation: Slippery-floor story: what goes wrong in one minute of a day with zero friction
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to narrate a frictionless morning (brushing, walking, writing); let them discover the problems

misconceptions.belief: Gravity acts only on falling objects.
signs: Says a book on a shelf has no gravity on it
Thinks a ball at the top of its throw has no gravity
Thinks gravity 'switches on' when things fall

diagnostic.prompt_en: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top, when it stops for a moment, is gravity acting on it?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Gend seedhi upar phenki. Sabse upar jab woh ek pal ke liye rukti hai, kya us pe gravity lag rahi hai?

options.text: No, gravity acts only when it falls
Yes, gravity acts on it all the time; that is why it comes back down
No, the throw cancels gravity at the top

remediation.representation: Strobe picture of a ball thrown up with a downward gravity arrow drawn at every position
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to draw the gravity arrow at each point, including the top and when it rests in a hand

misconceptions.belief: Non-contact forces need air or touching to work, so there is no gravity in space.
signs: Says astronauts float because there is no gravity
Thinks magnets cannot act through glass or water
Says the Moon is held by air

diagnostic.prompt_en: Why does the Moon keep going around the Earth instead of flying away?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Chaand Dharti ke chaaron or kyon ghoomta rehta hai, door kyon nahi chala jaata?

options.text: There is no gravity in space, so it just drifts
Earth's gravity pulls on the Moon across empty space
Air between the Earth and the Moon holds it

remediation.representation: Ball on a string swung in a circle: let go of the string and the ball flies off
remediation.moveShape: Map the string to gravity; ask what would happen to the Moon if gravity switched off

items.prompt_en: Classify each as a contact or non-contact force: a magnet pulling a pin; pushing a door; a rubbed comb attracting paper bits; brakes slowing a cycle; a mango falling from a tree.
items.prompt_hi: Har ek ko contact ya non-contact force mein baanto: magnet ka pin kheenchna; darwaaza dhakelna; ghise hue kanghe ka kaagaz ke tukde kheenchna; brake se cycle ka dheema hona; ped se aam ka girna.
items.answer: Contact: pushing a door (muscular), brakes slowing a cycle (friction). Non-contact: magnet pulling a pin (magnetic), comb attracting paper (electrostatic), mango falling (gravitational).
acceptable: door and brakes contact; magnet, comb, mango non-contact
hints: Ask which ones need touching
Point to the gap between the magnet and the pin
Prompt: magnet, comb and mango are ___
Assert: two contact, three non-contact

items.prompt_en: Name two ways to reduce friction and two ways to increase it, with an example of each.
items.prompt_hi: Friction kam karne ke do aur badhaane ke do tareeke batao, udaharan ke saath.
items.answer: Reduce: oil or grease in door hinges and cycle chains; ball bearings or wheels (a suitcase on wheels). Increase: treads on shoes and tyres; sprinkling sand on a slippery path; a rubber grip on a bat handle.
hints: Ask what is put on a squeaky door hinge
Point to the bottom of sports shoes
Prompt: reduce with ___; increase with ___
Assert: lubricants and wheels reduce; treads and grip increase

items.prompt_en: Predict: a ball is rolled at the same speed on a grass lawn and on a cement floor. On which does it stop sooner, and why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek gend ko ek jaisi raftaar se ghaas pe aur cement ke farsh pe ludhkaaya. Kahan jaldi rukegi, aur kyon?
items.answer: On the grass, because its rough, uneven surface gives much more friction against the ball than smooth cement.
hints: Ask which surface is rougher
Point to friction acting against the ball
Prompt: more friction on ___, so it stops ___
Assert: grass, because of more friction

items.prompt_en: Predict: on a dry day, you rub a plastic comb through dry hair, then hold it just above tiny bits of paper without touching them. What happens? Is this a contact or non-contact force?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: sookhe din, plastic ka kangha sookhe baalon mein ghis kar kaagaz ke chhote tukdon ke theek upar, bina chhue, rakhte ho. Kya hoga? Yeh contact force hai ya non-contact?
items.answer: The paper bits jump up to the comb. Rubbing gives the comb an electric charge, and this electrostatic force is a non-contact force.
hints: Ask what rubbing does to the comb
Point to the gap between comb and paper
Prompt: the charged comb pulls without ___
Assert: electrostatic, non-contact

items.prompt_en: Predict: you throw a ball straight up. At the very top, when it stops for a moment, is gravity still acting on it?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: gend seedhi upar phenkte ho. Sabse oonchi jagah, jab woh ek pal rukti hai, kya gravity tab bhi lag rahi hai?
items.answer: Yes. Gravity acts on it all the time; that is exactly why it slowed down on the way up and comes back down.
hints: Ask why the ball slowed down going up
Point to what makes it come back
Prompt: gravity acts on the ball ___ the time
Assert: yes, gravity never switches off

items.prompt_en: You said the ball stops sooner on grass because of friction. Why would we be in trouble if there were no friction at all?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha ghaas pe friction ki wajah se gend jaldi rukti hai. Agar friction bilkul na ho toh hum mushkil mein kyon pad jaayenge?
items.answer: We could not walk (our feet would slip), hold things, write with a pen, or stop a cycle with brakes; knots would come undone and screws would loosen.
hints: Ask what keeps their feet from slipping
Point to the pen and the brakes
Prompt: without friction we could not ___ or ___
Assert: friction is needed for walking, gripping and braking

items.prompt_en: Contrast the force a magnet uses to pull a pin with the force you use to open a door. Name each type and say what each needs in order to act.
items.prompt_hi: Magnet ke pin kheenchne wale force aur tumhare darwaaza kholne wale force ki tulna karo. Dono ka type batao aur dono ko kaam karne ke liye kya chahiye.
items.answer: The magnet's pull is a non-contact magnetic force; it acts across a gap. Opening the door uses a contact (muscular) force; your hand must touch the door.
hints: Ask whether the magnet touches the pin
Point to the hand on the handle
Prompt: magnetic is ___; muscular is ___
Assert: magnet acts at a distance; the push needs touch

items.prompt_en: Why do tyres and shoe soles have grooves (treads)? Is friction helping or harming here?
items.prompt_hi: Tyre aur jooton ke talve mein khaanche (treads) kyon hote hain? Yahan friction madad kar raha hai ya nuksaan?
items.answer: Treads increase grip (friction) and push water out from under the tyre or shoe on wet roads, so we do not slip. Here friction is helping.
hints: Ask what happens on a wet floor in smooth slippers
Point to the grooves pushing water away
Prompt: treads ___ friction so we don't ___
Assert: treads add grip; friction is useful here

items.prompt_en: Nothing touches the Moon, yet it keeps going around the Earth instead of flying off into space. Why?
items.prompt_hi: Chaand ko kuch nahi chhoota, phir bhi woh Dharti ke chaaron or ghoomta rehta hai, space mein door kyon nahi chala jaata?
items.answer: Earth's gravity, a non-contact force, pulls on the Moon all the time across empty space, bending its path into an orbit, like a string keeping a whirled ball moving in a circle.
hints: Ask what keeps a whirled ball on a string from flying off
Point to gravity as the invisible string
Prompt: ___ pulls the Moon even across empty space
Assert: Earth's gravity holds the Moon in orbit

items.prompt_en: Make a two-column chart, 'Contact' and 'Non-contact', and put one example from a cricket match in each column.
items.prompt_hi: Do column ka chart banao, 'Contact' aur 'Non-contact', aur har column mein cricket match ka ek udaharan likho.
items.answer: Contact: the bat hitting the ball, or friction slowing the ball on the outfield. Non-contact: gravity pulling the ball back down after a six.
acceptable: bat hits ball contact; gravity non-contact
hints: Invite them to picture one ball in a match
Point to the ball coming down after a big hit
Prompt: bat on ball is ___; gravity on the ball is ___
Assert: hitting is contact; gravity is non-contact

items.prompt_en: Golu writes, 'Friction is always bad. Engineers should remove it everywhere.' Correct him.
items.prompt_hi: Golu likhta hai, 'Friction hamesha bura hai. Engineers ko ise har jagah se hata dena chahiye.' Use theek karo.
items.answer: Friction is often useful: it lets us walk, grip, write and brake. Engineers reduce it where it causes wear and heat (with oil and ball bearings) and increase it where grip is needed (tyres, shoe soles).
hints: Ask what brakes rely on
Point to shoes on a wet floor
Prompt: reduce friction in ___, increase it in ___
Assert: friction is useful and harmful; engineers control it

items.prompt_en: Riya says, 'Gravity acts only when things fall. A book on a shelf has no gravity on it.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Riya kehti hai, 'Gravity sirf girti cheezon pe lagti hai. Shelf pe rakhi kitaab pe gravity nahi lagti.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: Gravity acts on the book all the time; the shelf pushes up with an equal force, so the forces balance and the book stays still. Remove the shelf and it falls at once.
hints: Ask what happens if the shelf is pulled away
Point to the shelf pushing up
Prompt: gravity acts ___; the shelf ___ it
Assert: gravity is always on; the shelf balances it

items.prompt_en: Explain to a friend the difference between contact and non-contact forces, with two examples of each, and why friction is both a friend and a problem.
items.prompt_hi: Ek dost ko contact aur non-contact force ka fark samjhao, dono ke do udaharan ke saath, aur friction dost bhi hai aur pareshaani bhi, kyon.
items.answer: Key ideas: contact forces need touching (muscular, friction, a surface's push); non-contact forces act across a gap (magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational); gravity acts on everything all the time, even across empty space; friction opposes motion and depends on the surfaces; it helps us walk, grip and brake but causes wear and heat; we reduce it with oil and wheels and increase it with treads.
hints: Invite them to start with 'touching or not touching'
Point to friction's two sides
Prompt: friction helps us ___ but also causes ___
Assert: two families of forces; friction is useful and wasteful

items.prompt_en: From last time: name the three non-contact forces.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: teen non-contact forces ke naam batao.
items.answer: Magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces.
hints: Ask about the comb and the paper
Point to the falling mango and the magnet
Prompt: magnetic, ___ and ___
Assert: magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational

workedExample.problem: Why does a ball rolling on grass stop sooner than one rolling on a cement floor?
steps: Name the force acting against the rolling ball: friction from the surface (plus a little air resistance)
Compare the surfaces: grass is rough and uneven; cement is smooth
Rougher surfaces give more friction, so the backward force on the ball is bigger on grass
A bigger backward force slows the ball faster, so it stops sooner
Conclude: friction depends on the surfaces in contact; less friction means the ball travels farther
fadedVersion: The force acting against the ball is ___
Grass is ___; cement is smooth
Rougher surfaces give ___ friction
A bigger backward force makes the ball stop ___
Friction depends on the ___ in contact

skills.title: Tell mass (amount of matter, in kg) from weight (pull of gravity, in N)
Explain upthrust and why objects feel lighter in water
Predict floating or sinking by comparing an object's weight with the upthrust from the water it can push aside

expectations: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it is the same everywhere.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object, measured in newtons; on Earth 1 kg weighs about 10 N, and on the Moon an object weighs about one-sixth as much while its mass stays the same.
A liquid pushes up on an object in it; this upward push is called upthrust (buoyant force), so objects feel lighter in water.
The upthrust equals the weight of the liquid the object pushes aside (displaces): Archimedes' principle.
An object floats if the upthrust becomes equal to its weight before it is fully under water; otherwise it sinks.
Shape matters: a hollow steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water, while a solid steel ball of the same mass sinks.

misconceptions.belief: Mass and weight are the same thing.
signs: Says 'my weight is 40 kg' and treats it as a force
Thinks mass changes on the Moon
Uses kg and N interchangeably

diagnostic.prompt_en: An astronaut with a mass of 60 kg goes to the Moon. What happens?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: 60 kg mass wala astronaut Chaand pe jaata hai. Kya hota hai?

options.text: Her mass becomes 10 kg
Her mass stays 60 kg, but her weight becomes about one-sixth of her Earth weight
Both her mass and her weight stay the same

remediation.representation: Two instruments: a beam balance (same reading on the Moon) and a spring balance (lower reading on the Moon)
remediation.moveShape: Ask what each instrument really compares; let the child predict both Moon readings

misconceptions.belief: Heavy objects always sink and light objects always float.
signs: Predicts a big log will sink
Predicts a tiny pin will float
Explains floating only by weight

diagnostic.prompt_en: A huge wooden log and a small iron nail are dropped into a river. What happens?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek bahut bada lakdi ka latthha aur ek chhoti lohe ki keel nadi mein giraaye. Kya hota hai?

options.text: The heavy log sinks and the light nail floats
The log floats and the nail sinks; floating depends on more than weight
Both sink because they are solid

remediation.representation: Float-sink table with columns for weight, size and result, including a ship and a pin
remediation.moveShape: Sort surprises (heavy floaters, light sinkers); ask what else besides weight is changing

misconceptions.belief: Objects feel lighter in water because water takes away some of their mass, or because gravity is weaker under water.
signs: Says the mug 'loses weight' in water
Thinks gravity stops under water
Cannot name the upward push

diagnostic.prompt_en: Why does a mug full of water feel lighter while you lift it under water in a bucket?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Bucket ke andar paani se bhara mug utthaate waqt halka kyon lagta hai?

options.text: The water reduces its mass
The water pushes up on it (upthrust), so you need less force
Gravity does not work under water

remediation.representation: Arrow diagram: same-size weight arrow in air and water, plus an upthrust arrow in water
remediation.moveShape: Ask the child to push an empty bottle down into a bucket and describe the push back on their hand

items.prompt_en: A bag of rice has a mass of 5 kg. About how much does it weigh on Earth, in newtons? (Take 1 kg to weigh about 10 N.)
items.prompt_hi: Chaawal ke bag ka mass 5 kg hai. Dharti pe iska weight lagbhag kitne newton hoga? (1 kg ka weight lagbhag 10 N maano.)
items.answer: About 50 N (5 × 10 N; more exactly about 49 N).
hints: Ask what 1 kg weighs in newtons
Point to multiplying by 5
Prompt: 5 × 10 = ___ N
Assert: about 50 N

items.prompt_en: A 60 kg astronaut goes to the Moon, where gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's. What is her mass there, and about how much does she weigh there?
items.prompt_hi: 60 kg ka astronaut Chaand pe jaata hai, jahan gravity Dharti ki lagbhag chhathi hissa hai. Wahan uska mass kitna hai, aur weight lagbhag kitna?
items.answer: Her mass is still 60 kg. Her weight is about 600 N on Earth and about 100 N on the Moon (600 ÷ 6).
hints: Ask whether she loses any matter on the trip
Point to her Earth weight first
Prompt: mass stays ___ kg; weight = 600 ÷ 6 = ___ N
Assert: 60 kg; about 100 N

items.prompt_en: Predict: a stone hangs from a rubber band. What happens to the stretch of the band when you lower the stone into a bucket of water?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek patthar rubber band se latka hai. Patthar ko paani ki bucket mein utaarne pe rubber band ka khinchaav kya hoga?
items.answer: The band stretches less, because the water's upthrust pushes the stone up, so the band has to hold up less.
hints: Ask what the bucket water does to things in it
Point to the band carrying less load
Prompt: water pushes ___, so the band stretches ___
Assert: less stretch because of upthrust

items.prompt_en: Predict which will float and which will sink in a bucket of water: a big wooden log, a small iron nail, a plastic bottle cap, a steel spoon.
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo bucket mein kaun tairega aur kaun doobega: bada lakdi ka latthha, chhoti lohe ki keel, plastic ki bottle ka dhakkan, steel ki chammach.
items.answer: The log and the plastic cap float; the nail and the spoon sink.
acceptable: log and cap float; nail and spoon sink
hints: Ask whether size alone decides
Point to what the objects are made of
Prompt: wood and plastic ___; iron and steel ___
Assert: log and cap float; nail and spoon sink

items.prompt_en: Predict: a ball of plasticine (modelling clay) sinks in water. If you shape the same lump into a thin, wide bowl, will it float? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: plasticine ki goli paani mein doob jaati hai. Usi tukde ko patli, chaudi katori ki shape do, toh kya tairegi? Kyon?
items.answer: Yes, the bowl can float. Its new shape pushes aside much more water before going under, so the upthrust can grow to equal its weight.
hints: Ask whether its weight changed
Point to how much water the bowl pushes aside
Prompt: the bowl displaces ___ water, so upthrust can equal its ___
Assert: yes; shape changes the upthrust it can get

items.prompt_en: You said the stone seemed lighter in water. Its mass did not change, so why did it seem lighter?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha patthar paani mein halka laga. Uska mass toh nahi badla, phir halka kyon laga?
items.answer: The water pushes up on it with upthrust. Gravity still pulls with the same weight, but the upthrust supports part of it, so the band (or your hand) holds up less.
acceptable: upthrust supports part of the weight
hints: Ask what pushes back when you press a ball under water
Point to two forces: weight down, upthrust up
Prompt: the same weight, but ___ pushes up

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger friend why the wind blows, using the beach as your example.

items.answer: Key ideas: the Sun heats land faster than water; air over warm land expands, becomes less dense and rises; this leaves low pressure; cooler, denser air from over the sea (higher pressure) moves in; that moving air is the sea breeze; at night it reverses; wind always blows from high to low pressure; the monsoon is the same idea on a huge scale.
hints: Invite them to start with the Sun
Point to the hot sand and the cool sea
Prompt: air rises over the ___, and air from the ___ moves in
Assert: uneven heating makes pressure differences that drive wind

items.prompt_en: From last time: does wind blow from high to low pressure, or from low to high?
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: hawa high se low pressure ki taraf bahti hai ya low se high?
items.answer: From high pressure to low pressure.
hints: Ask about the cycle tube valve
Point to H and L
Prompt: from ___ to ___
Assert: high to low

workedExample.problem: Why does a cool breeze blow from the sea on a hot afternoon?
steps: The Sun shines on both the land and the sea
The land heats up faster than the sea water
Air above the hot land warms, expands, becomes less dense and rises, leaving low pressure near the ground
Air over the cooler sea is denser, at higher pressure
Air moves from high to low pressure, so a breeze blows from the sea to the land: a sea breeze

skills.title: Describe how thunderstorms and lightning form and why lightning is seen before thunder is heard
Describe how a cyclone forms over a warm sea and its parts: eye, eye wall, storm surge
List and justify safety measures during lightning and cyclones

expectations: In hot, humid weather, warm moist air rises quickly, cools, and its water vapour condenses into tall storm clouds.
Inside these clouds, moving ice and water particles separate electric charges; lightning is a giant spark between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground.
Thunder is the sound of air heated suddenly by lightning and expanding; light travels much faster than sound, so we see the flash first; every 3 seconds of delay is about 1 km.

Cyclones form over warm oceans (around 26-27 °C or warmer): rising moist air creates a low-pressure centre, more air rushes in and spirals because of the Earth's rotation, and heat released by condensation keeps it growing.
The calm, low-pressure centre is the eye; the strongest winds and heaviest rain are in the eye wall; storm surges flood coasts.

Lightning safety: go inside a building or a closed car; avoid tall trees, poles, open fields, water and metal; if caught in the open, crouch low. Cyclone safety: follow IMD warnings, move to shelters and stay there until officials say it is safe, because the calm eye is not the end.

misconceptions.belief: It is safe to shelter under a tall tree during lightning.
signs: Runs to a tree when it rains
Thinks trees 'protect' from lightning
Shelters under an isolated tree in a field

diagnostic.prompt_en: You are in a park when thunder and lightning start. Where is the safest place to go?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Tum park mein ho aur bijli kadakne lagti hai. Sabse surakshit jagah kaunsi hai?

options.text: Under the tallest tree
Inside a proper building or a closed car; if there is none, crouch low away from trees
An open hilltop, holding an umbrella

remediation.representation: Side view of a field: lightning striking a lone tree, with current spreading through the ground around it
remediation.moveShape: Ask why lightning tends to hit the tree; let the child see that standing near it puts them in the path

misconceptions.belief: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
signs: Feels safe where lightning struck before
Thinks a struck object 'used up' its electricity
Ignores lightning conductors

diagnostic.prompt_en: A tall mobile tower was struck by lightning last week. Is it now safe from lightning?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek oonche mobile tower pe pichhle hafte bijli giri thi. Kya ab us pe bijli nahi giregi?

options.text: Yes, lightning never strikes the same place twice
No; tall, pointed structures can be struck many times, which is why they have lightning conductors
Yes, because it used up its electricity

remediation.representation: Tall building with a lightning conductor guiding repeated strikes safely into the ground
remediation.moveShape: Ask why tall buildings carry conductors if one strike were enough; connect height to repeated strikes

misconceptions.belief: When the wind calms in the middle of a cyclone, the storm is over.
signs: Wants to go outside when it goes quiet
Does not know what the eye is
Ignores official all-clear messages

diagnostic.prompt_en: During a cyclone, the wind suddenly drops and the sky clears a little. What should a family in a shelter do?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Cyclone ke dauraan achaanak hawa ruk jaati hai aur aasmaan thoda saaf hota hai. Shelter mein baitha parivaar kya kare?

options.text: Go out, because the storm is over
Stay in the shelter; this may be the eye, and strong winds will return from the other direction
Go to the beach to see the waves

remediation.representation: Top-down cyclone map with a village passing through the eye wall, the eye, then the other side of the wall
remediation.moveShape: Move the village marker across the cyclone and ask what the wind does at each step

items.prompt_en: You see a lightning flash and hear the thunder 9 seconds later. About how far away was the lightning?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne bijli ki chamak dekhi aur 9 second baad garaj suni. Bijli lagbhag kitni door thi?
items.answer: About 3 km (9 ÷ 3 = 3, because sound travels about 1 km in 3 seconds).
hints: Ask how far sound goes in 3 seconds
Point to dividing the seconds by 3
Prompt: 9 ÷ 3 = ___ km
Assert: about 3 km

items.prompt_en: Name three parts or features of a cyclone and say what each is like.
items.prompt_hi: Cyclone ke teen hisse ya features batao aur har ek kaisa hota hai.
items.answer: The eye: a calm centre with very low pressure. The eye wall: a ring of the strongest winds and heaviest rain around the eye. Rain bands: spiral bands of cloud and rain. Storm surge: sea water pushed onto the coast.
hints: Ask what is at the very centre
Point to the ring around the centre
Prompt: the calm centre is the ___; around it is the ___
Assert: eye, eye wall, rain bands, storm surge

items.prompt_en: Predict: in north India, are thunderstorms more likely on a cool, dry winter day or on a hot, humid afternoon in May or June? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: uttar Bharat mein aandhi-toofaan thandi sookhi sardi ke din zyada hote hain ya May-June ki garam, umas bhari dopahar mein? Kyon?
items.answer: On the hot, humid afternoon. Warm, moist air rises fast, cools and forms tall storm clouds that can produce lightning.
hints: Ask what the air needs to build tall clouds
Point to heat and moisture
Prompt: warm ___ air rises fast and forms tall ___
Assert: hot, humid afternoons breed thunderstorms

items.prompt_en: Predict: would a cyclone form over the icy sea near Antarctica or over the warm Bay of Bengal? Why?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: cyclone Antarctica ke paas ke barfeele samundar pe banega ya garam Bay of Bengal pe? Kyon?
items.answer: Over the warm Bay of Bengal. Cyclones need warm sea water (around 26-27 °C or more) to supply the heat and moisture that make air rise and keep the storm growing.
hints: Ask what fuels the rising air
Point to warm water evaporating
Prompt: cyclones need ___ sea water
Assert: warm seas feed cyclones

items.prompt_en: Predict: a cyclone crosses the Odisha coast and its eye passes over a village. What will people notice as the eye arrives, and what comes after?
items.prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek cyclone Odisha ke tat se guzarta hai aur uska eye ek gaon ke upar se jaata hai. Eye aane pe log kya mehsoos karenge, aur uske baad kya hoga?
items.answer: As the eye arrives the wind drops, the rain eases and the sky may clear for a while. Then the other side of the eye wall arrives, with violent winds from the opposite direction, so people must stay sheltered.
hints: Ask what lies all around the eye
Point to the village moving out of the eye
Prompt: calm in the eye, then the ___ returns from the ___ side
Assert: the calm is temporary; the storm returns

items.prompt_en: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
items.prompt_hi: Hum bijli pehle kyon dekhte hain aur garaj baad mein kyon sunte hain?
items.answer: Light travels nearly a million times faster than sound (about 3 lakh km per second against about 340 m per second), so the flash reaches us almost at once while the sound takes time.
hints: Ask which is faster, light or sound
Point to the delay in seconds
Prompt: light travels much ___ than sound
Assert: light arrives first because it is far faster

items.prompt_en: You said not to shelter under a tall tree. Why is it dangerous?
items.prompt_hi: Tumne kaha oonche ped ke neeche nahi chhupna chahiye. Yeh khatarnaak kyon hai?
items.answer: Lightning tends to strike tall objects. The current can jump from the tree to a person standing close to it, or spread through the ground around it.
hints: Ask what lightning tends to hit first
Point to the ground around the tree
Prompt: lightning strikes ___ things and current can ___ to you
Assert: tall trees attract strikes that can reach you

items.prompt_en: Contrast sheltering in a closed car with a metal roof and sheltering in an open-sided bus stop or a tent during a lightning storm.
items.prompt_hi: Bijli wale toofaan mein metal chhat wali band car mein rukne aur khule bus stop ya tent mein rukne ki tulna karo.
items.answer: A closed metal car is fairly safe: its metal body carries the current around the people inside to the ground (keep windows shut and do not touch metal parts). An open shelter or a tent gives almost no protection.
hints: Ask where the current goes in a metal car
Point to the open sides of the bus stop
Prompt: the car's metal body carries current ___ the people
Assert: closed car is safer; open shelters and tents are not

items.prompt_en: You are playing cricket on an open ground when thunder rumbles. What should the team do, and how long should they wait before playing again?
items.prompt_hi: Khule maidan mein cricket khel rahe ho aur garaj sunaai deti hai. Team ko kya karna chahiye, aur dobara khelne se pehle kitna intezaar?
items.answer: Stop at once and go into a proper building or closed vehicles; stay away from trees, metal poles and the open pitch. Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back out.
hints: Ask whether hearing thunder means lightning is near enough to strike
Point to the safe shelters nearby
Prompt: go ___, and wait ___ minutes after the last thunder
Assert: indoors now; 30 minutes after the last rumble

items.prompt_en: In 1999 a super cyclone killed about 10,000 people in Odisha. In 2019 Cyclone Fani was also very strong, but far fewer people died after more than a million were moved to safety. What helped?
items.prompt_hi: 1999 mein ek super cyclone ne Odisha mein lagbhag 10,000 logon ki jaan li. 2019 mein Cyclone Fani bhi bahut taakatwar tha, par das lakh se zyada logon ko surakshit jagah le jaane ke baad bahut kam log mare. Kis cheez ne madad ki?
items.answer: Better science and planning: IMD tracked the cyclone with satellites and forecast its path and strength days ahead, warnings reached people early, cyclone shelters were ready, and large-scale evacuation moved people away from the coast and the storm surge.
hints: Ask how people knew Fani was coming
Point to shelters and evacuation
Prompt: ___ warnings and moving people to ___
Assert: forecasting, early warning and evacuation save lives

items.prompt_en: Describe a top-view diagram of a cyclone: label the eye, the eye wall and the spiral rain bands, and show which way the winds turn in the northern hemisphere.
items.prompt_hi: Cyclone ka upar se dikhne wala diagram batao: eye, eye wall aur ghumaavdar rain bands label karo, aur dikhao uttari golaardh mein hawaayein kis disha mein ghoomti hain.
items.answer: A clear calm circle at the centre (the eye), a thick ring of cloud around it (the eye wall), and spiral cloud bands curling outwards (rain bands). In the northern hemisphere the winds turn anticlockwise around the eye.
acceptable: eye in centre, wall around it
hints: Invite them to start at the centre
Point to the curl of the rain bands
Prompt: winds turn ___ in the northern hemisphere
Assert: eye, eye wall, rain bands; anticlockwise winds

items.prompt_en: Golu says, 'The tall temple tower was hit by lightning once, so standing next to it in a storm is the safest place now.' What is wrong?
items.prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai, 'Mandir ke oonche shikhar pe ek baar bijli giri thi, toh toofaan mein uske paas khada hona ab sabse surakshit hai.' Kya galat hai?
items.answer: Lightning can strike the same tall place again and again; that is why tall buildings use lightning conductors. Standing next to a tall structure in the open is dangerous; go inside a proper building instead.
hints: Ask why tall towers have lightning conductors
Point to height attracting strikes
Prompt: lightning can strike the same tall place ___
Assert: it can strike again; go indoors

items.prompt_en: Explain to your family what to do if a thunderstorm starts while you are outside, and what to do if a cyclone warning is issued, with a reason for each step.
items.prompt_hi: Apne parivaar ko samjhao ki bahar hote hue aandhi-toofaan shuru ho toh kya karein, aur cyclone ki chetaavni aaye toh kya karein, har kadam ka kaaran ke saath.
items.answer: Key ideas: lightning is a giant spark from charged storm clouds; it tends to strike tall objects; go into a building or a closed car; avoid trees, poles, open fields and water; crouch low if caught in the open; wait 30 minutes after the last thunder; cyclones form over warm seas around a low-pressure eye; follow IMD warnings, go to shelters early, store water and food, and stay sheltered even when the eye brings calm.
hints: Invite them to split the plan into lightning and cyclone
Point to the reason behind each step
Prompt: avoid tall trees because ___; stay in during the eye because ___
Assert: each safety step follows from how the storm works

items.prompt_en: From last time: name two places that are unsafe during lightning.
items.prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: bijli ke dauraan do asurakshit jagahein batao.
items.answer: Any two: under or near tall trees; open fields or grounds; hilltops; in or near water (ponds, pools); next to metal poles or fences.
hints: Ask about the lone tree in the park
Point to open ground and water
Prompt: under tall ___ and in open ___
Assert: tall trees, open fields, water, metal poles

workedExample.problem: How far away is the storm, and when is it safe to go out?
steps: When you see a flash, start counting seconds until you hear the thunder
Divide the seconds by 3 to get the distance in kilometres (sound covers about 1 km in 3 seconds)
If you can hear thunder at all, lightning is close enough to strike, so go indoors at once
Keep counting with each flash; a shorter gap means the storm is coming closer
Stay indoors until about 30 minutes after the last thunder
